title: Ada and the Interior
premise: Twelve years after walking out of the Halvorsen Conservatory on the night of her debut recital, Lior Winterbourne returns not as a pianist but as a janitor, mopping floors beneath the practice rooms where she once burned. When a radio broadcasts a song she wrote at nineteen and never recorded — a song only one other person ever heard — Lior discovers that her old teacher, Ada Voss, is dying and has been quietly giving the piece away to students as an inheritance of unfinished feeling. As Lior traces the song through the hands it has passed into, she must confront the stranger in the old photographs: the version of herself who chose silence over justice when Ada's compositions were stolen by the conservatory's director. In the end, Lior plays the song publicly at Ada's deathbed vigil, names the theft aloud, and finds that belonging was never granted by institutions but claimed in the act of speaking.
about_author: Hazel Vasquez is a former conservatory custodian turned novelist whose essays on music, labor, and memory have appeared in small literary journals across the Pacific Northwest. She writes from a converted practice room in Portland, where she keeps a piano she refuses to tune.

chapters.title: The Weight of Keys
chapters.summary: Lior, POV. Twelve years after abandoning her debut recital mid-phrase, Lior returns to Halvorsen Conservatory as a janitor, mopping beneath the practice rooms where she once lived for the piano. The emotional beat is quiet shame disguised as pragmatism — she tells herself this is penance, not retreat.

chapters.title: Static
chapters.summary: Lior, POV. Late shift, a radio left on in the empty recital hall plays a song Lior wrote at nineteen and never recorded — a piece only Ada Voss ever heard. She stands frozen with a mop in her hands as the melody unfolds note-perfect. The beat is vertigo: the past has been broadcast without permission.

chapters.title: The Stranger in the Photograph
chapters.summary: Lior, POV. Digging through a storage closet, Lior finds framed photographs of the 2009 masterclass — herself at nineteen beside Ada, both smiling, taken weeks before everything broke. She cannot recognize the girl who let the director steal Ada's compositions without protest. Beat: grief curdling into self-estrangement.

chapters.title: Practice Room 4
chapters.summary: Lior, POV. Lior learns a current student, Theo Nakamura, has been playing 'her' song all semester, told it was a gift from a dying teacher. She watches him rehearse through frosted glass, unable to enter. Beat: possessive fury warring with the recognition that the song sounds better in his hands.

chapters.title: What Ada Kept
chapters.summary: Theo, POV. Theo describes his lessons with Ada Voss — how she taught him the unnamed song measure by measure, saying only, 'This belongs to someone who couldn't carry it yet.' He senses the janitor watching him and leaves the practice room door open. Beat: innocent generosity, unknowing trespass.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Almost
chapters.summary: Lior, POV. A flashback braided with present: the night Lior discovered Director Emil Brandt had published three of Ada's pieces under his own name, and chose her career over testimony. She remembers practicing the art of almost saying it. Beat: the architecture of complicity laid bare.

chapters.title: The Visiting Hours
chapters.summary: Lior, POV. Lior visits Ada in a care facility by the river; Ada pretends not to know her, then says, 'You always did come back through the service entrance.' Neither apologizes. Beat: two people fluent in avoidance, circling the wound they share.

chapters.title: Brandt's Anniversary
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The conservatory celebrates Director Brandt's twenty-fifth anniversary; his keynote praises 'originality' while students perform the stolen works. Lior serves champagne in uniform, invisible. Beat: public erasure performed as celebration, rage compressed into servility.

chapters.title: The Second Copy
chapters.summary: Theo, POV. Theo finds a second manuscript of the song in Ada's donated papers — dated earlier, annotated in a young hand he doesn't recognize: Lior's. He begins asking questions the faculty deflect. Beat: curiosity hardening into investigation.

chapters.title: Dust and Ledger
chapters.summary: Lior, POV. Cleaning the archive room, Lior finds the original composition ledgers proving authorship — dates, drafts, Ada's marginal notes addressed to her. She photographs every page with shaking hands. Beat: evidence as inheritance; the law finally within reach, twelve years too late for comfort.

chapters.title: A Lawyer Who Plays Cello
chapters.summary: Lior, POV. Lior consults Miriam Okafor, a cellist-turned-copyright attorney, who explains the statute of limitations has likely closed but moral claims and institutional pressure remain possible. 'Justice outside the law,' Miriam warns, 'costs more than the legal kind.' Beat: hope complicated by price tags.

chapters.title: Interlude: What the Song Is About
chapters.summary: Ada, POV. From the care facility, Ada remembers writing nothing — the song was Lior's, played to her once at midnight, and Ada kept it alive deliberately, passing it student to student like a message in a bottle waiting for its addressee. Beat: tenderness revealed as strategy; love as long patience.

chapters.title: Confrontation in Corridor B
chapters.summary: Lior and Theo, alternating. Theo corners Lior: 'It's yours, isn't it?' Lior denies it badly. Their argument cracks open her denial, and she admits the song, the theft, the silence — to a stranger first. Beat: confession as rehearsal for the real thing.

chapters.title: Brandt Offers a Hand
chapters.summary: Lior, POV. Brandt recognizes Lior, offers her a teaching post and co-credit on an upcoming recording of 'their' shared repertoire — hush money dressed as redemption. Lior almost accepts. Beat: temptation rendered generously; the reader understands why she once said nothing.

chapters.title: Ada Stops Speaking
chapters.summary: Theo and Lior, alternating. Ada suffers a stroke; her speech goes, though her hands still move on the blanket in rhythm. The doctors give her weeks. Lior realizes the window for reconciliation is closing faster than any lawsuit. Beat: urgency replacing deliberation.

chapters.title: The Vigil Organizes Itself
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Students begin holding nightly vigils in the recital hall, playing Ada's — truly Ada's — works. Theo proposes performing the unnamed song at the final vigil and crediting its true author. Lior must decide whether to stand behind the name or inside it. Beat: community as instrument of justice.

chapters.title: Ledgers Made Public
chapters.summary: Lior, POV. Lior sends the photographed ledgers to the board, the alumni newsletter, and Miriam — simultaneously, refusing negotiation. Brandt's allies circle; her janitorial job is threatened. Beat: the point of no return, chosen calmly, hands steady for the first time.

chapters.title: What the Board Cannot Unhear
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. An emergency board meeting leaks; former students come forward with corroborating memories. Brandt resigns 'for health reasons,' his anniversary portrait removed before the glue dries. Beat: vindication arriving without triumph — hollow, late, necessary.

chapters.title: Tuning
chapters.summary: Lior, POV. Alone in the recital hall at 3 a.m., Lior opens the piano she has cleaned around for months and plays for the first time in twelve years. Her hands remember everything, including the place she stopped. Beat: terror transfigured into homecoming; the body forgiving the mind.

chapters.title: The Last Vigil
chapters.summary: Lior, POV. At Ada's bedside vigil-turned-concert, Theo plays the opening measures, then stops and turns: 'It belongs to someone here.' Lior walks from the shadows in her janitor's uniform and finishes the song herself, announcing Ada's authorship of its survival and her own of its beginning. Beat: climax — the art of almost saying it, finally said.

chapters.title: Ada's Hands
chapters.summary: Lior, POV. Ada dies two days later, her fingers resting on the blanket in the shape of the song's final chord. At the funeral, the conservatory hangs Lior's photograph beside Ada's — the stranger in the old photographs, forgiven at last. Beat: mourning braided with peace; inheritance accepted.

chapters.title: Coda: The Interior
chapters.summary: Lior, POV. Months later, Lior teaches a Saturday class for kids who can't afford lessons, in Practice Room 4, and still mops the halls some nights because she likes knowing the building from below. She records the song at last and gives it away freely. Beat: resolution — belonging claimed, justice carried forward as gift rather than verdict.
